title: Only three layers of the Atlas are immutable, bounding permanence to the smallest workable core
content:
A.1.2.1 draws the immutability line by depth: "The first three layers contain the Immutable Documents, which together enshrine the Spirit of the Atlas and the core, permanent boundaries for how to operationalize it without risking slippery slope misalignment." Below them sit the Adaptive Documents, which "interpret and practically operationalize the Spirit of the Atlas within the boundaries set by the Immutable Documents."

The crucial detail is that the immutable layers fix **two** things, not one: the Spirit itself, and the boundaries on how it may be operationalized. Enshrining only the Spirit would leave the framework open to being operationalized into its opposite through individually reasonable Adaptive changes. Fixing the boundaries as well means the drift argument has to be won against explicit limits, not against a mood.

Why three layers rather than one or five is the engineering judgment. Too shallow and the permanent text is too abstract to constrain anything; too deep and the framework loses the ability to adapt to an environment it cannot predict. Three layers — Scope, Article, Section — gives roughly one layer of purpose, one of focus area, and one of discrete rule, which is why A.1.2.2.2.5 insists Section Documents be "atomized" to a single discrete unit of logic: permanence is only safe at a granularity fine enough that each locked statement can be judged on its own.
description: A.1.2.1 assigns the first three layers to Immutable Documents that fix the Spirit and its permanent operationalization boundaries; everything below is continuously improved within those boundaries.
